summary: This Standards Track document defines the eap.arpa. domain, used only in Network Access Identifiers, so an EAP peer can ask the server for limited, unauthenticated network access. Predefined identifiers in the NAI format of RFC 7542 say what kind of access is wanted. It updates RFC 5216, RFC 9140, and RFC 9190.

plainLanguage.summary: A new device usually has no credentials, so it cannot join the network to be given any. This RFC reserves a domain name that a device can send as its identity to ask for limited, unauthenticated access, and defines the registry of those identities.

questions: what is an eap provisioning identifier
subtitle: A reserved name that lets a device with no credentials ask a network for limited access, so that it can be provisioned.

tldr.problem: EAP normally needs the device to hold credentials before it can join the network, so a new device has no way to get the credentials it needs. The earlier specifications allowed unauthenticated access but gave the peer no way to ask for it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reserves the eap.arpa. domain for use in Network Access Identifiers and defines a registry of predefined identifiers. A peer sends one of them as its EAP identity, and a server that recognises it replies with the matching EAP method and limits the access it grants.
tldr.outcome: A device can now ask for limited access in a way the server can recognise. The document updates RFC 5216, RFC 9140 and RFC 9190, and deprecates the eap-noob.arpa domain in favour of @noob.eap.arpa.

facts.label: NAI length that fails with RADIUS

today: RFC 9965 is a Proposed Standard from May 2026. It updates RFC 5216, RFC 9140 and RFC 9190, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
In most uses of EAP, the peers must already hold pre-provisioned credentials. Without them a device cannot obtain network access, and so it cannot be provisioned with credentials. That is the bootstrapping problem this specification addresses. It creates a framework of predefined, well-known provisioning credentials and instantiates that framework for two mechanisms.

A client submits one of these predefined credentials to a server to obtain limited network access. The server, seeing a predefined credential, knows in advance that it is to be used only for provisioning, and can therefore avoid granting unrestricted network access to a peer that presents one. The device can then use the EAP channel itself for provisioning, as with the Tunnel Extensible Authentication Protocol described in RFC 9930, or the EAP server can give the device access to a limited captive portal, as in RFC 8952. Once the device is provisioned it uses the new credentials to obtain full network access.

The predefined provisioning credentials use a generic identity format. Identifiers in this space are called EAP Provisioning Identifiers, or EPIs. Because the identity is predefined and used only for unauthenticated network access, there is little benefit in specifying predefined passwords. Where the underlying EAP method allows it, this specification provides for password-less access, and where a password is required the password is defined to be the same as the identity.
sections.plainLanguage: A device with no credentials cannot join the network, and it cannot be given credentials without joining. This RFC breaks that circle by letting the device send a public, predefined identity that says it only wants enough access to be set up.

sections.title: What Earlier Specifications Already Allow
sections.content:
Both RFC 5216 and RFC 9190 provide for peer unauthenticated access, but neither defines a way for a peer to signal that it is asking for it. The presumption is that the peer connects with some value for the EAP Identity but does so without using a client certificate, and the server is then supposed to work out that unauthenticated access is wanted and limit the authorisation accordingly. The RFC notes that there appear to be no peer or server implementations that support such access, because no step of it is defined.

The Wi-Fi Alliance has defined an unauthenticated EAP-TLS method using a vendor-specific EAP method as part of HotSpot 2.0r2, but there appear to be few deployments of it. EAP-NOOB, described in RFC 9140, goes further: it defines both a way to signal that provisioning is desired and a way to exchange provisioning information inside EAP-NOOB, so the device does not need limited network access at all because all the provisioning happens within the protocol.

TEAP provides for provisioning over an unauthenticated TLS tunnel and has a server unauthenticated provisioning mode, but the inner TLS exchange still requires both ends to authenticate each other. There are ways to provision a certificate, but the peer must still authenticate itself with preexisting credentials, so any provisioning method that uses TEAP has to address that limitation.

The RFC groups provisioning into two kinds: provisioning done inside the EAP method, as with EAP-NOOB, and EAP used to obtain limited network access, as with a captive portal, after which IP-based provisioning runs over more complex protocols. Doing the provisioning inside EAP is often useful because the EAP and AAA administrators do not control the network, and it is not always possible to define a captive portal where provisioning can be done.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier documents allowed a server to give unauthenticated access, but never said how a device could ask for it or how the server should recognise the request. This RFC fills that gap with a public, registered name.

sections.title: The Realm and the Identity Format
sections.content:
A device with no credentials of its own uses a provisioning identifier in NAI format, as defined in RFC 7542. The NAI has two parts, the utf8-username and the utf8-realm, which this document calls the username and realm fields. The realm is chosen to be independent of, and unused by, any existing organisation, so that every organisation can use it, and it is one that no AAA proxy framework defined in RFC 7542 proxies automatically and one that returns no results for dynamic discovery, as described in RFC 7585. The specification does not forbid routing packets for NAIs in the eap.arpa realm, leaving that to individual organisations.

The realm field signals the behaviour being requested: the subdomain under the eap.arpa. domain distinguishes the different requested methods, and it is assigned through the EAP Provisioning Identifiers registry. Where possible the first subdomain should use the EAP method name from the Method Types registry, but those names do not follow the domain name format of RFC 7542, so where a direct mapping is impossible the chosen realm name must still be similar enough that the average reader can tell which EAP method is meant.

Extra subdomains are allowed, and they let vendors and Standards Development Organisations self-assign a delegated range of identifiers that cannot conflict with anyone else's. Any realm in the registry, such as tls.eap.arpa, implicitly defines a sub-realm v., such as v.tls.eap.arpa, and organisations can self-allocate inside it using realms they own, for example example.com.v.tls.eap.arpa. The specification makes no provision for private-use realms, because the v. sub-realm is enough for all private uses. Experimental provisioning methods must be defined inside the appropriate vendor's namespace, and inside IETF documents the ietf.org vendor space must be used, with different uses distinguished by working group or document name, such as emu.ietf.org.v.eap.arpa.

The username field depends on the EAP method being used, and it may be empty or hold a fixed value; EAP-NOOB for example uses the username noob. Other methods may omit the username, as RFC 7542 recommends. The name anonymous is not recommended for specifications using this format, even though RFC 7542 permits it, because it is widely used in NAIs today and would cause confusion. Since these names are defined in public specifications, user privacy does not apply to them and the username can be publicly visible.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity is a name with two parts. The realm part sits under eap.arpa and says which kind of setup the device wants. The username part is optional and depends on the method being used. Both parts are public, because the point is that anyone can recognise them.

sections.title: How Peers and Servers Use the Identifiers
sections.content:
An EAP peer signals that it wants a certain kind of provisioning by using an EPI together with an associated EAP method, and a separate specification defines the meaning of the identifier and the behaviour of the peer. The EPI must come from an entry in the EAP Provisioning Identifiers registry, and the EAP method used with that NAI must match the EAP method from the same entry. Where a peer allows local selection of a provisioning method, the identifier is chosen by the method rather than by the end user, so the peer must not have a configuration interface that lets the user type the identifier directly. A user who types an identifier that matches an EPI anyway is not a security problem: the user will either be rejected because the server does not support provisioning or be placed into a captive portal.

When everything works, the peer gains new credentials, drops its network connection and re-authenticates with the new credentials, usually without the user being involved. Provisioning can fail in several ways, and the peer must track which methods it has tried and not repeat the same method against the same server after an EAP Nak. Peers must rate limit their provisioning attempts: if provisioning fails it is likely because provisioning is not available, so retrying quickly is unlikely to change the server's behaviour and is likely to get the peer blocked. A peer should retry no more than once every few minutes, with jitter and exponential backoff, and should err on the side of long delays, since there is no way to tell a transient server failure from a server that does not support the method. It is recommended that a peer try the new credentials for network access as soon as it has them, so that errors show up quickly, and that it provision again before its current credentials expire, even though re-provisioning means dropping off the full network to reach the provisioning network.

On the server side, an EAP session begins with the server receiving an initial EAP-Request/Identity message, and a server implementing this specification must examine the identity to see whether it uses a realm under the eap.arpa realm. Processing of all other identities is unchanged. A malformed EPI must be answered with an EAP Failure as in RFC 3748, and an EPI the server does not recognise must be answered with an EAP Nak of type zero, which says that the requested provisioning method is not available. The same Nak of type zero is sent if the peer proposes an EAP method the server does not support or does not recognise as valid for that provisioning method. Once the server accepts the provisioning method, it replies with an EAP method that must match the one associated with the EPI, and the EAP process continues as in the state machine in RFC 3748.

Servers must treat peers using an EPI as untrusted, and once such a peer is authenticated it must be placed into a limited network such as a captive portal that does not permit unrestricted access. Implementations should be aware of methods that bypass simple blocking, such as tunnelling data over DNS. The RFC is explicit that a secure provisioning network allows only the expected traffic and blocks everything else, because blocking only selected bad traffic leads to substantial security failures. The limited network should also limit how long a device may stay on it, since provisioning should take seconds to tens of seconds, and should limit the amount of data transferred and the number of services available. Servers should rate limit provisioning attempts, limit how many peers are provisioned at the same time, use functionality such as the RADIUS Filter-Id attribute to limit access, and prevent peers in the limited network from communicating with each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The device sends the identifier as its EAP identity and names the EAP method that goes with it. The server looks up the identifier, and if it knows it, runs that method and puts the device on a restricted network where only the provisioning traffic is allowed.

sections.title: Interaction with EAP Methods
sections.content:
Some EAP methods need shared credentials, such as passwords, because both parties know the same secret. That covers EAP-MSCHAPv2, the Protected Extensible Authentication Protocol also known as PEAP, and EAP-pwd. Where password-based methods are used the password should be the same as the provisioning identifier, because there are few reasons to define a method-specific password. The same applies to TLS-based EAP methods such as EAP-TTLS and PEAP: where the method provides for an inner identity and inner authentication, the credentials used there should be the provisioning identifier for both the inner identity and any inner password. It is recommended that provisioning be done with a TLS-based EAP method, because TLS authenticates the server and protects the integrity and confidentiality of the data exchanged in the tunnel. It also lets EAP-TLS run a full EAP session while the peer has nothing more than a few Certification Authorities configured locally.

All provisioning methods defined in the eap.arpa. domain must define a way to authenticate the server, either at the EAP layer as with TLS-based methods or after network access has been granted, for example when credentials are provisioned over HTTPS. Where TLS-based EAP methods are used, implementations must still validate EAP server certificates in every situation other than provisioning, though a method that provisions over another protocol may let the peer skip that check. Whether or not the certificate is checked, the peer must treat the local network as untrusted.

For EAP-TLS this document defines the NAI portal@tls.eap.arpa, which lets EAP peers use unauthenticated EAP-TLS. Its purpose is to let a peer signal that it wants captive portal network access, which is the peer unauthenticated access of RFC 5216 and RFC 9190. That access must still authenticate the EAP server, for example with a server certificate, so using TLS with a well-known pre-shared key is generally not appropriate because it would not provide server authentication. A server that agrees to the request must put the device into a captive portal with limited access. The method is an improvement on existing captive portals, which are typically unsecured and unauthenticated, because using peer unauthenticated TLS proves the server is authentic, and 802.1X secures the link between the peer and the authenticator. The captive portal can advertise support for the eap.arpa. domain through an 802.11u realm.

For EAP-NOOB, the RFC recommends that servers accept both noob@eap-noob.arpa and @noob.eap.arpa as synonyms, and that peers try @noob.eap.arpa first and fall back to noob@eap-noob.arpa if that does not succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: Where the EAP method needs a shared secret, the secret is the identifier itself. The document also defines one identifier in detail, portal@tls.eap.arpa, which asks for a captive portal over EAP-TLS, where the server proves its identity with a certificate but the device does not have one.

sections.title: The Registries
sections.content:
Two registry updates define the eap.arpa. domain. The eap-noob.arpa entry in the .ARPA Zone Management registry has its usage field prefixed with (DEPRECATED) and a reference to this document added, and a new entry for the eap.arpa domain is added with the usage for provisioning within the Extensible Authentication Protocol framework. The Special-Use Domain Names registry gains an entry for eap.arpa. IANA has also been instructed to refuse further allocation requests directly within the .ARPA Zone Management registry for anything related to EAP; those allocations are to be made in the new registry instead.

The new EAP Provisioning Identifiers registry sits in the Extensible Authentication Protocol registry group and uses Expert Review. Each entry has an NAI in the format of RFC 7542, a Method Type taken from the Method Types registry, and a reference to where the identifier was defined. The initial values are @noob.eap.arpa for EAP-NOOB and portal@tls.eap.arpa for EAP-TLS.

The guidelines for the designated experts are detailed. The NAI is meant to describe both the method type and the purpose of the provisioning method, so that an administrator who meets an unfamiliar NAI can make a reasonable deduction about what is being requested; with a Method Type of name and a purpose of action, the NAI should be of the form action@name.eap.arpa. The NAI must satisfy the format of RFC 7542 Section 2.2, the utf8-username portion may be empty but must not be anonymous, and the NAI must be a subdomain within the eap.arpa realm. The identifiers are case-insensitive and must all be lowercase, and they must be unique when compared in that way. Entries should be short, because they are generally sent in the User-Name attribute of a RADIUS packet and implementations are likely to support a total NAI length of 63 octets, with lengths between 63 and 253 octets possibly working and lengths of 254 octets or more not working with RADIUS.

The Method Type must provide a Master Session Key and an Extended MSK as defined in RFC 3748, because without them it cannot be used in an authentication framework that requires those methods, such as 802.1X. Organisations can also self-allocate inside the v. sub-realm without an explicit allocation, using a domain name they have registered, for example local@example.com.v.tls.eap.arpa. Because DNS registrations can change over time and that change is unlikely to be reflected in shipped products, the RFC recommends that organisations avoid self-assigned realms, and may use them only when no alternative exists and when they expect to maintain operation for at least the lifetime of the devices that use them.
sections.plainLanguage: The names are kept in a public registry, so a server anywhere can look one up. The registry has rules about how a name is written and who may allocate one, and it starts with two entries.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The EAP Identity field is generally publicly visible to anyone who can observe the EAP traffic. The names used here are in a public specification, so exposing them within EAP carries no privacy implication. The goal of the specification is to make those names public so that unknown and private parties can publicly and anonymously declare what kind of network access they want.

There are many other privacy concerns around the specification. Most EAP traffic is sent over RADIUS, and RADIUS Access-Request packets typically contain a large amount of information such as Media Access Control addresses and device location. This specification does not change RADIUS or EAP, and so does not change which information is public or private; those issues are dealt with in other specifications. It can, however, increase privacy by letting devices obtain network access anonymously and then securely obtain credentials. The names here sit in a public registry, so they do not have to follow the username privacy recommendations of RFC 7542 Section 2.4, though other personally identifying information may still appear in EAP or AAA packets, which is no different from normal EAP authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifiers themselves carry no privacy cost, because they are published. The privacy question is elsewhere, in the RADIUS packets that carry them, which the RFC leaves to the other specifications that govern RADIUS.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The specification defines a framework that lets unknown, anonymous and unauthenticated devices request and obtain network access, so it is critical that operators give those devices limited access. Future specifications that define an NAI in the registry should describe in detail what kind of access is provided.

In most EAP use cases the server identity is validated, usually through a certificate, or the method binds the TLS tunnel cryptographically to the inner application data. The methods here use public credentials, or skip server validation, so on-path attacks succeed where they would normally fail. Peers and servers must assume that all data sent over an EAP session is visible to attackers and can be modified by them. The methods defined here must only be used to bootstrap initial network access; once a device is provisioned it gains access through the provisioned credentials and the usual network access policies apply.

Provisioning is unauthenticated, so like any unauthenticated process the access can be abused. The RFC lists the ways to secure the provisioning network: allow only the traffic the current provisioning method needs and block everything else, with the note that DNS recursive resolvers should not be made available because DNS has been used to exfiltrate traffic; limit the services available to those needed for provisioning; limit the number of devices on the provisioning network at the same time; rate limit each device's access; limit the total time a device may remain on the network; and limit the total amount of data it may transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole point is that a device with no credentials gets in, so the network it lands on has to be locked down. Only the traffic provisioning needs should be allowed, the number of devices should be capped, and each device should be limited in time and data.

viz.caption: What the peer and the server each do

cells: Uses the EPI that matches the provisioning method, and offers no way to type the identifier directly.
Checks whether the realm is under eap.arpa. All other identities are processed as before.
Tries another method, and does not repeat the same method against the same server after a Nak.
Answers with EAP Failure for a malformed identifier, or a Nak of type 0 for one it does not recognise.
Drops the connection and re-authenticates with the newly provisioned credentials.
Places the peer in a limited network, such as a captive portal, that allows only provisioning traffic.

viz.caption: The limits the RFC puts on the provisioning network

items.title: Only the needed traffic
items.text: Allow only what the current provisioning method needs and block everything else. DNS resolvers should not be available, because DNS has been used to exfiltrate traffic.

items.title: Only the needed services
items.text: Limit the services available on the provisioning network to the ones provisioning needs.

items.title: A limit on the number of devices
items.text: Limit how many devices can be on the provisioning network at the same time.

items.title: A rate limit per device
items.text: For any one device, rate limit its access to the provisioning network.

items.title: A limit on time
items.text: Limit the total time a device may stay on the provisioning network.

items.title: A limit on data
items.text: Limit the total amount of data a device may transfer through the network.
